title: Refused a Clerk's Job, Eli Lilly Opened a Laboratory on Pearl Street
dek: In spring 1876, after a second partnership went sour, Eli Lilly asked a wholesaler for a job; he was told to start his own firm instead, and opened with $1,400.

story.event: Leaving a failed partnership, being refused a clerk's job and opening a laboratory at 15 West Pearl Street with $1,400
story.summary: In March 1876 Eli Lilly left the Indianapolis drug-manufacturing partnership Johnston and Lilly with about $1,000 in cash and $400 in stock after finding his partner had drawn more than his share of the profits. When he asked the wholesale druggist Augustus Kiefer for a clerk's job, Kiefer refused, urged him to manufacture on his own and promised orders. Lilly opened at 15 West Pearl Street on 10 May 1876 with three employees, including his 14-year-old son, and sales nearly tripled in 1877.
paragraphs: On 27 March 1876, Eli Lilly gave up his share of Johnston and Lilly, the small drug-manufacturing firm he had run in Indianapolis since New Year's Day 1874 with a dentist, John F. Johnston. By the account in the company's own archive, Lilly had grown frustrated with his partner's lack of interest and then found that Johnston had drawn more than his half of the profits. Lilly asked only for what he had put in, and left with about $1,000 in cash and $400 in stock, a few gallons of fluid extracts.

He was 37, a pharmacist since a teenage apprenticeship in Lafayette and a Union Army veteran who had commanded an artillery battery, and this was not his first loss. After the Civil War he had leased a cotton plantation in Mississippi; drought ruined the crop, his partner made off with their money, and in August 1866 his wife, Emily, died there while eight months pregnant. A drugstore partnership in Paris, Illinois, had done well, but he had left it to make medicines rather than sell them.

Now, the archive says, he went to Augustus Kiefer, an Indianapolis wholesale druggist, and asked to be taken on as a clerk. Kiefer refused. He thought Lilly too good a manufacturer to work for anyone else, urged him to start on his own, promised him orders and asked other wholesalers in the city to back him too. Lilly accepted. He rented a two-storey building 18 feet wide and 40 deep at 15 West Pearl Street and opened on 10 May 1876 under a sign reading "Eli Lilly, Chemist." The $1,400 was all the capital he had.

He had three employees, one of them his 14-year-old son, Josiah, and the Indiana Historical Society records that they worked 72-hour weeks. Lilly aimed at physicians rather than the patent-medicine trade: he checked products for strength and purity, listed ingredients on labels and was among the first to put doses in gelatin capsules. Sales for the first eight months came to $3,477, by the society's count, and nearly tripled in 1877. The firm moved twice in four years, became a corporation around 1880 and, in 1905, under his son, reached $1 million in sales.

quote.text: Make not Man thy partner but Heaven, and making Heaven thy partner do thy best. Never condemn others; but see to it that thou comest not short of thine own mark.
quote.source_title: Bushido, the Soul of Japan, Project Gutenberg eBook #12096
quote.connection: After two partners had cost him dearly, Saigō's advice to make Heaven, not man, your partner might have sounded like hard-won sense to Lilly. Yet what put him in business was a man: a wholesaler who refused him a job and found him buyers. Being let down by people and carried by them happened in the same spring.

reflection: Asking Kiefer for a clerk's job was a reasonable thing to do. Lilly had lost a wife and a plantation, and money to two partners, and a steady wage would have been a sensible thing to want. The refusal is what changed his year, and it came from someone who could see his work more clearly than he could that week.

You may have days when the safer option looks like the only honest one, and sometimes it is. Before you decide, it is worth asking someone who knows your work well what they would do in your place, and actually listening to the answer.
invitation: Ask one person who has seen your work up close what they would do about the decision you are weighing, and let their answer sit until tomorrow before you act on it.

sources.title: Eli Lilly & Company (Hoosier business history)
sources.supports: Founded 10 May 1876 at 15 West Pearl Street, then 36 South Meridian (1878-81) and McCarty and Alabama Streets (1881-); Lilly and three other employees, including his fourteen-year-old son, working seventy-two hours a week; moving twice in four years; gelatin capsules to control dosage; checking strength and purity and listing ingredients on labels; focus on the 'ethical' market sold through medical professionals; first eight months' sales of $3,477 and $11,318.73 by the end of 1877; incorporation in 1880; sales of $1 million by 1905

cross_checks.claim: On 27 March 1876 Lilly left Johnston and Lilly with about $1,000 in cash and $400 in merchandise, roughly $1,400 in all.
The wholesale druggist Augustus Kiefer encouraged Lilly to start his own manufacturing business and arranged orders for it.
Lilly opened his laboratory at 15 West Pearl Street, Indianapolis, on 10 May 1876.
He started with three employees, one of them his 14-year-old son Josiah.
Sales nearly tripled in 1877, and the firm reached $1 million in sales by 1905.

research_notes: First-year sales disagree: the Indiana Historical Society gives $3,477 for the first eight months and $11,318.73 by the end of 1877, while Wikipedia gives $4,470 for 1876 (and $48,000 for 1879). The story uses the society's figure, attributed to it, and the 'nearly tripled in 1877' that the society and the Encyclopedia of Indianapolis both state. Kiefer's help: the Lilly Archives biography says Kiefer refused to employ Lilly, promised orders and solicited commitments from the other half-dozen local wholesalers; Wikipedia (spelling him 'Keifer') says two associated drugstores agreed to buy from Lilly below their current prices. The story follows the company archive in general terms ('asked other wholesalers in the city to back him') and uses the archive's spelling. The Indiana Historical Society places Lilly's short-lived manufacturing partnership in Paris, Illinois; the Lilly Archives and Wikipedia place Johnston and Lilly in Indianapolis and the Paris venture as a retail drugstore with James Binford; the story follows the archive. Incorporation: 1880 (Historical Society, Encyclopedia) against 1881 (Wikipedia); the story says 'around 1880'. Staff: the Historical Society's 'he and three other employees, including his fourteen-year-old son', the Encyclopedia's 'himself, his son and two other employees' and Wikipedia's three named employees agree on three employees. Lilly's age: born 8 July 1838, so 37 in March and May 1876; the archive's 'age of 38' is rounded. The 72-hour week is the Historical Society's statement alone and is attributed. No first-person words of Lilly about the decision were found, so none are quoted; his feelings are not described beyond the archive's account of his frustration. The quote is Saigō Takamori's saying as given in English by Nitobe, who wrote in English, so no translator is listed.
